::: {.callout-note title="Analogy: cutting a newspaper into clippings"}
To file a newspaper for later, you could cut it into strips every 10 centimetres. Fast, and every strip is the same size, but half of them start mid-sentence and end in the next article. Or you cut along the articles: each clipping is one story, with its headline on top. That takes knowing where the articles start, which is easy if you can read the layout.

Atlas's first chunker cut every file into 40-line strips. This lesson cuts along the layout: Python by its functions and classes, documents by their headings.
:::

## The problem

Since lesson 3.6, Atlas has split every file into blocks of 40 lines. Search returns those blocks, and lesson 6.7 will hand them to a model as the evidence for an answer. A block that starts in the middle of one function and ends in the middle of the next is poor evidence: half of what the model needs is missing, and the other half is about something else.

How often does that happen? Counted on Ignite at commit `0abbcab`, for every function and method (using Python's own parser to find where each one starts and ends):

```text
4397 functions and methods in Ignite's Python files
windows     2437 chunks,  36.9 lines on average, functions whole in one chunk: 3026 (69%)
```

Almost one function in three is cut in two. And a block has no name: search can say "lines 361 to 400 of `engine.py`" but not "this is `Engine.run`".

## Theory

### Chunk along structure

A **chunk** should be the smallest piece that makes sense on its own. Files already say where those pieces are:

| File | Structure | A chunk is |
|---|---|---|
| Python | functions, classes, methods | one top-level function; a class header (class line, docstring, class attributes); each method |
| Markdown | `#` headings (outside code blocks) | one section, named by its heading path (`Ignite > Installation`) |
| reStructuredText | underlined headings | one section, the same way |
| anything else | none Atlas understands | a 40-line window |

Every chunk records its **symbol**: the function, method or heading path it belongs to. Search results become `ignite/engine/engine.py:Engine.run`, and the embedding of each chunk is headed by its file and symbol (lesson 6.4), so a question mentioning "Engine" finds `Engine.run` even if the method's body never says the word.

Two practical rules:

- **Very long pieces are still cut**, into windows of at most 60 lines that keep the symbol. A 300-line method isn't one thought anyway, and long chunks blur embeddings.
- **Files that don't parse fall back to windows.** Half-written code, Python 2, templates: the chunker must never fail an index.

### Python's own parser: `ast`

Python ships with a parser for Python. `ast.parse(text)` turns source code into an **abstract syntax tree**: objects for each statement, with exact positions. A `def` becomes an `ast.FunctionDef` with `.name`, `.lineno` (its first line) and `.end_lineno` (its last). Decorators are separate (`.decorator_list`), and belong with their function, so a chunk starts at the first decorator.

```python
import ast

tree = ast.parse("@cache\ndef f(x):\n    return x\n")
node = tree.body[0]
print(type(node).__name__, node.name, node.lineno, node.end_lineno, node.decorator_list[0].lineno)
# FunctionDef f 2 3 1
```

Regular expressions can't do this reliably: a `def` inside a string, a multi-line signature, nested functions. The parser knows the language.

### Incremental re-indexing, now with vectors

Lesson 5.3 re-indexes only the files a commit changed. But a changed file is deleted and re-chunked whole, and every one of its chunks would then need a new embedding: at about 2 chunks a second on a CPU, a one-line change to a 100-chunk file costs most of a minute. Usually only one or two of its chunks actually changed. So before deleting a file's chunks, Atlas remembers their vectors by `(path, chunk text)`, and gives each new chunk the vector of an identical old one. Only genuinely new or edited chunks wait for the embed job.

```{mermaid}
flowchart TD
    F[Changed file] --> R[Remember old chunks' vectors<br/>by path and text]
    R --> D[Delete the file's old chunks]
    D --> P{Parse}
    P -->|.py| A[ast: functions, class headers, methods]
    P -->|.md / .rst| H[Headings]
    P -->|other, or a syntax error| W[40-line windows]
    A --> L[Cut pieces over 60 lines]
    H --> L
    W --> N[New chunks with symbols]
    L --> N
    N --> M{Same text as an old chunk?}
    M -->|yes| K[Keep its vector]
    M -->|no| E[Embed later, embed_repo job]
```

## In the project

### Red: what a chunker must do

`tests/test_chunking.py` describes the behaviour on small, readable inputs:

```python
PYTHON = '''"""Tools for training loops."""

import math

LIMIT = 10


@decorated
def top_level(x):
    """Double it."""
    return x * 2


class Engine:
    """Runs the loop."""

    retries = 3

    def __init__(self):
        self.state = None

    def run(self, data):
        for batch in data:
            self.step(batch)
        return self.state
'''


def test_python_is_split_at_functions_classes_and_methods() -> None:
    pieces = chunk_file("ignite/engine.py", PYTHON)

    assert spans(pieces) == [
        (None, 1, 5),  # module docstring, imports and constants (blank edges trimmed)
        ("top_level", 8, 11),  # the decorator belongs to the function
        ("Engine", 14, 17),  # class line, docstring and class attributes
        ("Engine.__init__", 19, 20),
        ("Engine.run", 22, 25),
    ]
    assert pieces[1].text.startswith("@decorated\ndef top_level(x):")
```

More tests: every non-blank line is in exactly one chunk; a 151-line function becomes three windows all named `huge`; broken code falls back to windows; Markdown splits at headings but not at a `#` comment inside a code fence; reStructuredText splits at underlined headings; YAML gets windows.

### Green: `atlas/chunking.py`

The Python part walks the module's top-level statements, turning definitions into spans and the code between them into unnamed module spans:

```python
def python_spans(text: str) -> list[Span] | None:
    try:
        tree = ast.parse(text)
    except SyntaxError:
        return None  # half-written or Python 2 code: line windows instead

    spans: list[Span] = []
    line_count = len(text.splitlines())
    next_free = 1  # first line not yet in a span
    for node in tree.body:
        if not isinstance(node, DEFINITIONS):
            continue
        start = first_line(node)
        if start > next_free:
            spans.append((None, next_free, start - 1))  # module-level code before it
        if isinstance(node, ast.ClassDef):
            spans.extend(class_spans(node))
        else:
            spans.append((node.name, start, last_line(node)))
        next_free = last_line(node) + 1
    if next_free <= line_count:
        spans.append((None, next_free, line_count))
    return spans
```

`class_spans` produces the class header (from the class line to just before its first method), each method as `Class.method`, and any class-level code between methods under the class's name. `chunk_file` then trims blank lines off each span's edges and cuts anything over 60 lines into windows.

For documents, both formats reduce to a list of headings, `(line, level, title)`, and one shared function turns them into sections named by their path:

```python
def sections(headings: list[tuple[int, int, str]], line_count: int) -> list[Span]:
    spans: list[Span] = []
    first_heading = headings[0][0] if headings else line_count + 1
    if first_heading > 1:
        spans.append((None, 1, first_heading - 1))
    path: list[tuple[int, str]] = []  # (level, title) of the enclosing headings
    for index, (line, level, title) in enumerate(headings):
        path = [entry for entry in path if entry[0] < level]
        path.append((level, title))
        end = headings[index + 1][0] - 1 if index + 1 < len(headings) else line_count
        spans.append((" > ".join(name for _, name in path), line, end))
    return spans
```

Markdown headings are `#` to `######` at the start of a line, skipped inside ```` ``` ```` fences. reStructuredText marks a heading by underlining it with a repeated character, and the order in which underline characters first appear in a file sets the levels, so the first one seen (`=`, in all ten of Ignite's `.rst` files) is level 1.

`storage.read_document` now builds chunks from `chunk_file`, storing each piece's `symbol` (migration `0010` added the column). The `chunk_lines` parameter is gone, along with lesson 3.6's `split_into_chunks`; two storage tests changed their expectations, deliberately: the sample `engine.py` now gives the chunks `Engine` and `Engine.run` instead of line pairs, and the search for "fire event" returns the whole `Engine.run` method (lines 2 to 3) instead of one line.

### Measured on Ignite

```text
4397 functions and methods in Ignite's Python files
windows     2437 chunks,  36.9 lines on average, functions whole in one chunk: 3026 (69%)
structure   4631 chunks,  18.0 lines on average, functions whole in one chunk: 4202 (96%)
```

96% of functions now sit whole in one chunk; the rest are longer than 60 lines (or nested inside such a function), and are cut into named windows on purpose. The price: twice as many chunks, so twice as many embeddings to compute and store, and half the average size. Re-indexing Ignite with the new chunker:

```text
$ atlas index --path ~/code/ignite --repo pytorch/ignite
indexed 403 files into 4631 chunks (0 skipped) as pytorch/ignite
```

### Red, then green: keeping unchanged vectors

```python
def test_reindexing_keeps_the_embeddings_of_unchanged_chunks(
    session: Session, factory: sessionmaker[Session], sample_repo: Path
) -> None:
    storage.index_folder(session, "pytorch/ignite", sample_repo)
    embed_pending(factory, FakeEmbeddings(), repo_id(session))
    engine = sample_repo / "ignite" / "engine" / "engine.py"
    # Change Engine.run; leave the class line, accuracy and the README alone.
    engine.write_text(engine.read_text().replace("self.fire_event", "self.fire"))

    storage.update_index(
        session, "pytorch/ignite", sample_repo, changed=["ignite/engine/engine.py"], deleted=[]
    )

    still_missing = session.scalars(select(Chunk.symbol).where(Chunk.embedding.is_(None))).all()
    assert still_missing == ["Engine.run"]
```

In `storage.py`, `update_index` (and `index_folder`, for full re-indexes) now remembers vectors before deleting:

```python
def stored_embeddings(session: Session, repo_id: int, paths: list[str] | None) -> StoredEmbeddings:
    """The vectors of chunks about to be deleted, so unchanged ones can keep theirs (6.5)."""
    ...


def reuse_embeddings(document: Document, kept: StoredEmbeddings) -> None:
    """Give each new chunk the vector of an identical old chunk in the same file, if any.

    Embedding is the slow, costly step of indexing; a one-line change to a file shouldn't
    mean re-embedding every function in it.
    """
    for chunk in document.chunks:
        previous = kept.get((document.path, chunk.text))
        if previous is not None:
            chunk.embedding, chunk.embedding_model = previous
```

`chunk.embedding, chunk.embedding_model = previous` assigns both values of the pair at once (**tuple unpacking**). The vector keeps its model name, so a vector from an old model is reused as "pending" and the embed job replaces it.

On Ignite, re-syncing from 30 commits back (lesson 5.3's experiment, now with vectors):

```text
index at ce87844: 4596 chunks, 0 without a vector
sync to 0abbcab: 66 files re-indexed into 1026 chunks in 2.2 s
after: 4631 chunks, 142 without a vector
  1.7 min: 142 embedded, 0 remaining, 1.37 chunks/s
```

The 30 commits touched 66 files. Re-indexing them produced 1026 chunks, and 884 of those were identical to a chunk in the old version of their file, so they kept their vectors. Only 142 needed the model: 1.7 minutes instead of the 29 a full embed takes. Without `reuse_embeddings`, all 1026 would have been pending, about seven minutes at the same rate.

## Trade-offs *(deep dive)*

**Chunk size.** Smaller chunks match questions more precisely and give the model less noise; larger ones carry more context. Functions are a natural unit for code; 60 lines caps the long tail.

**Overlap.** Window chunkers often overlap neighbouring windows by some lines, so a sentence cut at a boundary appears whole in one of them. Structural chunks rarely need it, because their boundaries are meaningful.

**Context in the chunk.** Atlas adds the file and symbol to what's embedded. Some systems go further and add a model-written summary of the surrounding file to each chunk; better retrieval, at the cost of a model call per chunk.

**Other languages.** `ast` only parses Python. Tools such as tree-sitter parse many languages with one interface; Atlas would add them as files of those languages appear in tracked repositories. Until then, they get windows.

## Common mistakes

- **Fixed-size windows for code.** Functions get cut in half; chunks have no names.
- **Splitting on regular expressions.** A `def` in a string or a `#` in a code fence fools them; use a parser.
- **Failing the whole index on one unparseable file.** Fall back to windows.
- **Unlimited chunk sizes.** One 400-line method becomes one blurry vector; cut and keep the name.
- **Re-embedding unchanged chunks.** Reuse vectors by content.
- **Forgetting decorators.** They're part of the function.

## Check yourself

**1.** A chunk boundary falls between `@dataclass(frozen=True)` and `class Hit:`. What goes wrong, and how does the chunker avoid it?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The decorator would land in the previous chunk (or a module chunk) and `Hit`'s chunk wouldn't show that it's a frozen dataclass, which changes what the class does. The chunker starts each definition at its first decorator's line (`first_line` uses `decorator_list`), so decorators always travel with what they decorate.
:::

**2.** Why does a file that fails to parse get windows instead of being skipped?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Its text is still searchable and may hold the answer to a question (a half-finished example, a Python 2 script, a template). Skipping it would silently hide it from search; windows are worse chunks, but chunks.
:::

**3.** A commit changes one line in a file with 40 chunks. How many chunks does the embed job have to embed?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Usually one: the chunk containing the changed line gets new text and so no reused vector; the other 39 have the same `(path, text)` as before and keep theirs. More, if the change moves a boundary (a new function, a renamed heading) and so changes the text of neighbouring chunks.
:::

## Exercise

Chunk Ignite's `ignite/engine/engine.py` with `chunk_file` and print its five longest chunks, with their symbols and line ranges. What do you notice about their sizes, and why?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution"}
```python
from pathlib import Path
from atlas.chunking import chunk_file

pieces = chunk_file("ignite/engine/engine.py", Path("ignite/engine/engine.py").read_text())
print(len(pieces), "chunks")
for p in sorted(pieces, key=lambda p: p.end_line - p.start_line, reverse=True)[:5]:
    print(f"{p.end_line - p.start_line + 1:>3} lines  {p.start_line:>4}-{p.end_line:<4} {p.symbol}")
```
```text
53 chunks
 60 lines    20-79   Engine
 60 lines   166-225  Engine.register_events
 60 lines   279-338  Engine.add_event_handler
 60 lines   479-538  Engine.interrupt
 60 lines   562-621  Engine.terminate
```
All five are exactly 60 lines: each is the first window of a piece longer than `MAX_LINES`, cut and named after it. Even the `Engine` class header is, because its docstring (with usage examples) is longer than 60 lines. Long docstrings are common in well-documented libraries; that's where most of the cut pieces in the 4% come from. (At commit `0abbcab`.)
:::

## Stretch

Methods can contain nested functions (helpers defined inside a method). Write a test showing what the chunker does with one, and decide whether that's the right behaviour.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution"}
```python
def test_a_nested_function_stays_in_its_method() -> None:
    source = "class A:\n    def m(self):\n        def helper():\n            return 1\n        return helper()\n"

    pieces = chunk_file("a.py", source)

    assert [(p.symbol, p.start_line, p.end_line) for p in pieces] == [("A", 1, 1), ("A.m", 2, 5)]
```
It passes against the reference code: `class_spans` only looks at a class's direct children, so `helper` stays inside `A.m`'s chunk. That's right: a nested helper only makes sense with the method that uses it, and splitting it out would separate the call from the definition. Not in the reference code.
:::

## What changed in the project

New `atlas/chunking.py` (`chunk_file`: Python by `ast`, Markdown and reStructuredText by headings, windows otherwise); `chunks.symbol`; `read_document` uses it, `split_into_chunks` and `chunk_lines` removed; `stored_embeddings` and `reuse_embeddings` keep unchanged chunks' vectors on re-index; `tests/test_chunking.py`, and updated storage and API tests. Commit: `feat: Added structural chunking, embeddings in pgvector and a sliced embed_repo job`.
